Thought Leadership That Sales Can Use

The Commercial SystemPart 11

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 9-minute read · Growth

In short: Thought leadership pays when a seller can use it in a conversation to help a buyer decide, and most of it is never used that way. The evidence on buying points to why that use matters: Gartner's 2026 survey found confident buyers were twice as likely to report a high-quality deal, and Challenger's analysis of 2.5 million sales calls found around half of lost deals ended in no decision. A published position becomes usable when it is converted into five things a seller can carry: a discovery question, a diagnostic, a business case line, an objection answer and a first step. The loop closes when what sellers hear flows back into the positions.

Key points

  • A point of view earns its cost in the sales conversation, not in impressions.
  • Buyers need decision confidence: Gartner found confident buyers twice as likely to report a high-quality deal.
  • Around half of lost deals end in no decision, so the main competitor is often the buyer's own uncertainty.
  • One position should convert into five sales tools: a question, a diagnostic, a business case line, an objection answer and a first step.
  • Win-loss evidence should feed the positions: one vendor's research finds 77% of factors that drove buyers' decisions never came up in sales calls.

Part 9 gave each piece of content a job. Thought leadership has the hardest job of all: to change how a buyer thinks about a problem before they have decided to buy anything. That makes it the most difficult content to connect to revenue, and the easiest to cut when budgets tighten.

Our explainer What thought leadership actually is sets out the standard a piece has to meet: a specific claim, evidence the audience could not gather alone, a practical consequence and consistency over time. This part assumes that standard is met. Its subject is what happens next: how a position that passes the test reaches the conversations where deals are won and lost.

The gap between the byline and the call

In most firms, thought leadership and selling are run by different people on different calendars. Marketing publishes a position; sales may read it, may share it on social media, and rarely uses it in a meeting. Buyers notice the disconnect. Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 B2B buyers found 69% reported inconsistencies between what a supplier's website said and what its sellers told them.

The sales side has its own overload. Gartner's 2023 survey of 501 sellers found 77% struggled to complete their assigned tasks efficiently, and 82% of sales leaders said enablement content or delivery needed to change significantly to meet revenue goals. Forrester found reps choosing from an average of 1,400 sales assets. Adding a thought leadership article to that pile does not help. Converting it into something a seller can say in a meeting does.

What buyers need from a point of view

The case for thought leadership in sales rests on how buyers decide, and the recent evidence is consistent.

Buyers say it opens the door. In the same Edelman and LinkedIn study, 95% of hidden buyers said strong thought leadership makes them more receptive to sales and marketing outreach. The study is run by a communications agency and a platform that sells B2B advertising, so read it as direction rather than measurement.

Buyers form preferences early. 6sense's 2024 Buyer Experience Report found buyers nearly 70% of the way through their process before contacting a seller, with 81% already holding a preferred vendor at first contact. Whatever shapes the buyer's view of the problem in that period shapes the shortlist.

Buyers need confidence more than information. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 buyers found confident buyers were twice as likely to report a high-quality deal than buyers with low decision confidence. Gartner frames the seller's task as "value clarity": a clear understanding of how a solution improves outcomes in the buyer's specific role and context. A position that explains the problem in the buyer's own terms is the raw material for that.

The main competitor is indecision. Challenger's research on 2.5 million recorded sales calls found around half of lost deals ended in no decision. Its analysis found win rates of 6% where buyer indecision was high, against 30% where it was medium. Buyers stall when they are unsure the problem is real, unsure which approach is right, or afraid of getting it wrong. Each of those is a question a good point of view answers.

Thought leadership that only shapes opinion stops at the shortlist. Thought leadership that sales can use carries on into the decision.

Five tools from one position

A single published position, if it meets the standard above, contains everything a seller needs. The work is to extract it into forms that fit a conversation.

Part of the positionSales toolWhere it is usedTest of whether it works
The claimA discovery question that tests whether the claim applies to this buyerFirst and second meetingsThe buyer answers with specifics, not a polite yes
The evidenceA diagnostic the buyer can run on their own numbersBetween meetings, often shared internallyThe buyer comes back with a result
The consequenceOne line for the business case, with the cost of inactionProposal and sponsor's internal pitchThe line appears in the buyer's own documents
The disagreementAn answer to the most likely objectionWhenever a sceptic joins the buying groupThe objection stops recurring
The Monday actionA first step for the mutual planCommit stageThe step is agreed and dated

Take an illustrative position from a firm that sells commercial advisory work: "most mid-size firms report pipeline coverage without the win rate behind it, so their boards cannot tell whether the pipeline is enough." Converted:

  • Question: "When your board sees pipeline coverage, does it also see the win rate and cycle length that make it meaningful?"
  • Diagnostic: a one-page calculation the buyer runs to find the coverage they actually need, given their own win rate and cycle.
  • Business case line: the gap between reported and required coverage, expressed as bookings at risk.
  • Objection answer: for "our coverage rule has always worked," a short explanation of the one case where three times coverage holds, and how often it does not.
  • First step: restate last quarter's coverage with its win rate before the next board meeting.

None of those needs a new piece of content. All of them need someone to do the extraction, test it with two or three sellers, and keep it current. The diagnostic is usually the most valuable, because it gives the buyer something to take to colleagues the seller will never meet. Forrester's 2024 research found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, so a tool that travels without the seller does much of the work. Edelman and LinkedIn's 2025 study of nearly 2,000 professionals points the same way: among the buying group members it calls hidden buyers, 71% said they had little or no interaction with sales teams, and 52% of hidden decision-influencers said high-quality thought leadership helps them persuade other members of the buying group.

Sales feeding the positions

The loop has to run both ways. Positions written from the marketing team's view of the market drift away from what buyers actually say. Positions written from sales evidence stay close to it.

Win-loss evidence is the best source, and it routinely surprises firms. In a 2026 interview published by Showpad, the co-chief executive of win-loss provider Clozd cited its research finding that 85% of CRM loss reasons did not match what buyers said drove their decision, and that 77% of the factors that influenced decisions never came up in sales conversations. Those are vendor figures and should be read as such, but the direction matches the experience of most firms that interview buyers. Our explainer on win-loss analysis covers how to run the interviews.

InputWho supplies itHow oftenWhat it changes
Questions buyers ask that the firm cannot yet answer wellSellersWeekly, in pipeline reviewCandidate topics for new positions
Objections that recurSellers and sales leadershipMonthlyThe objection answer, or the position itself
Win-loss interview themesWhoever runs win-lossQuarterlyWhich positions to strengthen, retire or start
Language buyers use for the problemCall notes and recordingsOngoingThe words the position and its tools use

The founder interview method we have described elsewhere is one way to turn this evidence into publishable positions. The point here is the direction of flow: sales evidence in, positions out, tools back to sales.

Each position should sit in a single ledger with its claim, its evidence, its five tools, its owner and its review date. When a position changes, the tools change with it, and the change is recorded like any other commercial decision. That is the practical answer to Gartner's 69% inconsistency figure: one source for what the firm believes, read by marketing and sales alike.

Measuring by position, not by piece

Measuring thought leadership by the piece leads back to impressions. Measuring by the position, across every piece and tool that carries it, connects it to deals.

Four signals do most of the work. Use: the share of open opportunities where a seller used one of the position's tools, taken from the CRM. Echo: whether buyers repeat the position's language in their own emails, briefs or requests for proposal, which is the clearest evidence that it shaped their thinking. Progression: whether opportunities where the diagnostic was run moved through the next stage faster. No-decision rate: whether deals where the position was used stall less often than those where it was not.

Volumes will be small and the comparison is not a controlled test, so read these over two or three quarters as direction. Part 10 sets out what it would take to test them properly. The aim is modest: to know which positions sellers use and which buyers repeat, so that the next position is chosen on evidence. Our piece Dissent is the data you are throwing away makes the related case for recording the objections, not just the agreements.

Illustrative example: one position, five tools
Decision
Convert the firm's best-performing published position into a discovery question, a buyer-run diagnostic, a business case line, an objection answer and a mutual plan step, and track use in the CRM for two quarters.
Reason and owner
Sellers shared the article but never used it in meetings, and win-loss interviews showed deals stalling at the sponsor's internal pitch. Owned by the head of marketing, with two senior sellers testing each tool before release.
What changed
The diagnostic became the most attached asset in mid-stage deals, buyers began quoting its result in their own business cases, and two objection answers were rewritten after the first quarter.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B advisory and services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Aim at the decision. A point of view should help the buyer decide, not just admire the firm.
  • Extract five tools. Question, diagnostic, business case line, objection answer and first step.
  • Build tools that travel. The diagnostic reaches the buying group members the seller never meets.
  • Run the loop both ways. Sales evidence and win-loss themes should choose the next position.
  • Measure the position. Use, echo, progression and no-decision rate, read over quarters.
Gateway card

Before you publish the next position

  • A claim that a seller can test with one discovery question
  • A diagnostic a buyer can run on their own numbers
  • One business case line with the cost of inaction
  • An answer to the most likely objection
  • A first step that fits a mutual plan
  • An owner, a review date and a place in the position ledger

Common questions

How do you use thought leadership in sales?

Convert each published position into tools a seller can carry: a discovery question, a diagnostic the buyer runs, a business case line, an answer to the main objection and an agreed first step.

How do you measure the ROI of B2B thought leadership?

Measure by position rather than by piece: how often sellers use its tools in open deals, whether buyers repeat its language, whether those deals progress faster, and whether they stall less often.

Why do so many B2B deals end in no decision?

Buyers stall when they are unsure the problem is real, which approach fits or whether they will get it wrong. Challenger's research on 2.5 million sales calls found around half of lost deals ended in no decision.

How should sales and marketing work together on thought leadership?

Sales supplies the questions, objections and buyer language that choose and shape each position; marketing turns positions into tools; both work from a single ledger of what the firm believes.
